titleStmt.title: Conceptual knowledge OR Procedural knowledge OR Conceptual knowledge AND Procedural knowledge:Why the conjunction is important for teachers

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Conceptual knowledge OR Procedural knowledge OR Conceptual knowledge AND Procedural knowledge:Why the conjunction is important for teachers

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: critique
span.quote: For example, the false positioning of procedural and conceptual knowledge as being two extremes of a continuum, rather than them having the capacity to occupy different places on that continuum depending on the situation, does little to acknowledge their complexity.

span.label: conceptual and procedural knowledge in mathematics teaching
span.quote: The terms conceptual knowledge and procedural knowledge are often used by teachers and never more so than when discussing how teachers teach, and children learn mathematics.

span.label: review
span.quote: A thorough synthesis of extant and seminal literature will provide advice to teachers and teacher educators on how a deeper insight into conceptual and procedural knowledge could improve the quality of mathematics teaching.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: once procedures have been memorised and practised without understanding, students lose the motivation to look for their meaning, which is why a procedure-first sequence blocks the conceptual half of the iteration
span.quote: who asserted that once students have memorised and practised procedures (including written algorithms, that they do not necessarily understand) they have less motivation to comprehend their meaning or the reasoning behind them.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: acquiring procedural knowledge reduces the load on working memory, and the freed capacity can then be spent on building conceptual knowledge
span.quote: There is also evidence that gaining procedural knowledge can lessen the cognitive demands on working memory. This lessening of demand can then free the working memory to focus on conceptual knowledge development

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: a powerful earlier understanding (e.g. reading the equals sign as 'give me an answer') obtrudes into later learning and obfuscates the teaching that follows
span.quote: Cognitive interference, considered by Pesek and Kirshner as being the more important interference, is when previous understandings of something are so poweful they obtrude into subsequent learning.

span.label: The paper's claim that misunderstanding of the two knowledge forms is widespread among teachers rests on anecdote rather than on collected data.
span.quote: Anecdotally there is a good deal of misinformation regarding the efficacy of both knowledge forms amongst teachers, and this is unhelpful.

span.label: The paper concedes that the concept-first iterative approach it endorses has little empirical evidence behind it.
span.quote: With little empirical evidence to support a concept- first iterative approach, why then has it enjoyed such a pervasive adoption?

span.label: The dichotomy the paper's title turns on is reported as having been declared fundamentally unsound, on the ground that procedures are conceptual in nature.
span.note: what this limits: the conceptual/procedural split as a sound partition: the paper reports Kieran declaring the dichotomy fundamentally unsound because procedures are conceptual during elaboration
span.quote: Kieran (2013) declared the dichotomy between them to be fundamentally unsound. Kieran (2013) writes that “…during any period of elaboration, procedures are conceptual in nature

span.label: Treating the two knowledge forms as two ends of a continuum is called false; the paper holds that either can occupy different positions depending on the situation.
span.note: what this limits: a placement of a task or a learner at one end of the conceptual/procedural continuum: the paper calls that positioning false, since either can occupy different places depending on the situation
span.quote: the false positioning of procedural and conceptual knowledge as being two extremes of a continuum, rather than them having the capacity to occupy different places on that continuum depending on the situation

span.label: Two cells of Star's own matrix have no worked exemplars - the paper reports that deep-procedural and shallow-conceptual knowledge are hard even to illustrate.
span.quote: it is challenging to determine an illustration or articulation of deep-procedural, or shallow-conceptual knowledge

span.label: conceptual knowledge
span.quote: although the relationship between conceptual and procedural knowledge is bi-directional, it is not always symmetrical, and that, at times, conceptual knowledge is stronger and more consistent in supporting procedural knowledge, than the reverse.

span.label: procedural knowledge
span.quote: Procedural knowledge is characterised by some researchers (Canobi, 2009; Miller & Hudson, 2007; Rittle-Johnson & Schneider, 2015) as the capacity to follow steps in sequence to solve mathematical problems or reach a mathematical goal.

span.label: concept
span.quote: According to Westwood (2008) a concept can be defined as “a mental representation that embodies all the essential features of an object, a situation, or an idea. Concepts enable us to classify phenomena as belonging, or not belonging, together in certain categories

span.label: Relational Knowledge
span.quote: Conceptual knowledge (notably characterised by Skemp, 1978, as Relational Knowledge

span.label: routine expertise
span.quote: This reconceptualisation of Star’s (2005) model included constructs which they called, routine expertise, and adaptive expertise

span.label: adaptive expertise
span.quote: Adaptive expertise is where both conceptual and procedural knowledge is deep, and where that knowledge can be aplied creatively, flexibly and appropriately to all situations, familiar or new

span.label: CRA
span.quote: CRA, which in the literature is also referred to as CPA (Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract)

span.label: CPA

span.label: conceptual knowledge → procedural knowledge
span.note: THE DISTINCTION ITSELF IS DECLARED UNSOUND, and no type can say that. Kieran (2013) 'declared the dichotomy between them to be fundamentally unsound'. `distinct-from` asserts the two ARE distinct; there is no way to record a cited author denying that the boundary can be drawn - the same gap quine1951 sits in.
span.quote: Kieran (2013) declared the dichotomy between them to be fundamentally unsound

span.label: procedures → concepts
span.note: THE CATEGORIES INTERPENETRATE RATHER THAN RELATE: 'during any period of elaboration, procedures are conceptual in nature'. Not `is-a`, not `part-of`, not `same-as` - a claim that membership is temporary and phase-dependent, which no edge type carries.
span.quote: during any period of elaboration, procedures are conceptual in nature

span.label: concept - a mental representation embodying the essential features of an object, situation or idea, whose function is to let phenomena be classified as belonging together or not
span.quote: According to Westwood (2008) a concept can be defined as “a mental representation that embodies all the essential features of an object, a situation, or an idea. Concepts enable us to classify phenomena as belonging, or not belonging, together in certain categories

span.label: procedural knowledge - characterised by some researchers as the capacity to follow steps in sequence to reach a mathematical goal
span.quote: Procedural knowledge is characterised by some researchers (Canobi, 2009; Miller & Hudson, 2007; Rittle-Johnson & Schneider, 2015) as the capacity to follow steps in sequence to solve mathematical problems or reach a mathematical goal.

span.label: the conceptual/procedural relation - bi-directional but NOT always symmetrical, with conceptual knowledge at times the stronger support
span.quote: although the relationship between conceptual and procedural knowledge is bi-directional, it is not always symmetrical, and that, at times, conceptual knowledge is stronger and more consistent in supporting procedural knowledge, than the reverse.

span.label: conceptual/procedural - a single distinction carrying eight different name pairs across eight traditions (Skemp's instrumental/relational, Tulving's episodic/semantic, Anderson's procedural/declarative...), which the paper asserts are the same division
span.quote: In the past, the terms have been couched differently (Table 1), but regardless of the labels, the divisions regarding the types of knowledge are consistent

span.label: deep - in Star's matrix a property that BOTH knowledge types can have, not a property of conceptual knowledge alone
span.quote: The matrix indicates that for each knowledge type (conceptual and procedural) there is the possibility of developing a superficial knowledge or a deep knowledge

span.label: adaptive expertise - both knowledge types deep AND applicable to unfamiliar situations; routine expertise is the same knowledge without the transfer
span.quote: Routine expertise is where there is a superficial conceptual and/or procedural knowledge, which is able to be applied to familiar situations, but not unfamiliar ones, or to new tasks. Adaptive expertise is where both conceptual and procedural knowledge is deep, and where that knowledge can be aplied creatively, flexibly and appropriately to all situations, familiar or new

span.label: contradicts → the belief, held by the experienced teachers the author surveyed, that conceptual and procedural knowledge are mutually exclusive and that conceptual is always the more necessary
span.note: The paper's target is a belief held by practitioners rather than a published claim, and it is quoted from the author's own observation of them.
span.quote: the teachers indicated that they carried the belief that conceptual and procedural knowledge were mutually exclusive, and that conceptual knowledge was, without exception, more appropriate or necessary than procedural knowledge

span.label: conceptual knowledge —renamed-across-fields→ Relational Knowledge
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — An in-text renaming attributed to a named source: 'notably characterised by Skemp, 1978, as Relational Knowledge'.
span.quote: Conceptual knowledge (notably characterised by Skemp, 1978, as Relational Knowledge

span.label: conceptual knowledge —renamed-across-fields→ Declarative
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — TABLE 1 IS THIS PROJECT'S THESIS WITH A TABLE. Eight research traditions across 1976-1984 - Skemp, Piaget, Gelman & Gallistel, Resnick, Tulving, Anderson, Van Lehn, Baroody - each name the SAME two categories differently, and the paper says so outright: 'regardless of the labels, the divisions regarding the types of knowledge are consistent'. The claim of sameness is the paper's, not the tagger's.
span.quote: In the past, the terms have been couched differently (Table 1), but regardless of the labels, the divisions regarding the types of knowledge are consistent. (Hiebert & Lefevre, 1986). span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — TABLE 1 IS THIS PROJECT'S THESIS WITH A TABLE. Eight research traditions across 1976-1984 - Skemp, Piaget, Gelman & Gallistel, Resnick, Tulving, Anderson, Van Lehn, Baroody - each name the SAME two categories differently, and the paper says so outright: 'regardless of the labels, the divisions regarding the types of knowledge are consistent'. The claim of sameness is the paper's, not the tagger's.
span.quote: Research is unambiguous in accepting that both conceptual knowledge and procedural knowledge are important (Hiebert & Grouws, 2007; Rittle-Johnson, Schneider & Star, 2015). This acceptance that both forms of knowledge are important allows the debate to move to determining the relationship between the two. Although this debate still receives contemporary attention (Alcock et al., 2014; Rittle-Johnson, 2017; Rittle-Johnson & Koedinger, 2009; Schneider, Rittle-Johnson & Star, 2011) it is one that has some history (e.g. Resnick & Ford, 1981; Sowder, 1998). In the past, the terms have been couched differently (Table 1), but regardless of the labels, the divisions regarding the types of knowledge are consistent. (Hiebert & Lefevre, 1986). span.label: CRA —same-as→ CPA
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — 'also referred to as' - one instructional sequence, two acronyms live in the same literature.
span.quote: CRA, which in the literature is also referred to as CPA (Concrete-Pictorial-Abstract)

span.label: conceptual knowledge —contrasted-with→ procedural knowledge
span.note: differs in: NOT depth, which is the assumption the paper is attacking: Star's matrix gives each knowledge type its own superficial and deep form, so `deep` is a second dimension rather than a synonym for `conceptual` · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: The matrix indicates that for each knowledge type (conceptual and procedural) there is the possibility of developing a superficial knowledge or a deep knowledge

span.label: adaptive expertise —contrasted-with→ routine expertise
span.note: differs in: whether the knowledge transfers to unfamiliar situations - routine expertise applies to familiar ones only · strength of the relation: 0.8
span.quote: Routine expertise is where there is a superficial conceptual and/or procedural knowledge, which is able to be applied to familiar situations, but not unfamiliar ones, or to new tasks. Adaptive expertise is where both conceptual and procedural knowledge is deep, and where that knowledge can be aplied creatively, flexibly and appropriately to all situations, familiar or new

span.label: Experienced primary and lower-secondary teachers believed that conceptual and procedural knowledge are mutually exclusive and that conceptual knowledge is always the more appropriate thing to teach.
span.quote: In essence, the teachers indicated that they carried the belief that conceptual and procedural knowledge were mutually exclusive, and that conceptual knowledge was, without exception, more appropriate or necessary than procedural knowledge.

span.label: Both procedural and conceptual knowledge matter and each reinforces the other, so teaching should aim at both rather than choosing between them.
span.quote: Procedural knowledge and conceptual knowledge are both important and help to strengthen each other.

span.label: Either knowledge type can be shallow or deep, so treating conceptual as inherently deep and procedural as inherently shallow misrepresents both.
span.quote: Both procedural and conceptual knowledge are more nuanced structures than many teachers realise. Both can be ‘shallow’ (superficial) or ‘deep’.

span.label: The synthesis endorses teaching conceptual knowledge before procedural knowledge in most cases.
span.quote: Conceptual knowledge in most cases should precede procedural knowledge.

span.label: Starting with conceptual knowledge and moving to procedural knowledge makes conceptual understanding more likely, whereas the procedural-to-conceptual direction risks students never reaching conceptual knowledge.
span.quote: There is more chance of students developing a conceptual knowledge if they start with conceptual knowledge and then move to procedural knowledge.

span.label: The empirical support for concept-first is that students taught conceptually and then procedurally outperform students taught procedurally and then conceptually.
span.quote: students who are taught for a conceptual understanding followed by a procedural understanding, outperform students who are instructed for procedural then coneptual knowledge (Pesek & Kirshner, 2000).

span.label: Procedural practice only feeds conceptual growth when the problems are sequenced to expose conceptual relationships; randomly ordered problems produced no such effect.
span.quote: Research (Canobi, 2009; McNeil et al., 2012) showed how sequencing arithmetic problems to encourage the identification of conceptual relationships proved to be efficacious, whereas when the problems were in random order this effect was not noted.

span.label: The conceptual-procedural relationship is bi-directional but asymmetric: conceptual knowledge supports procedural knowledge more strongly and more consistently than procedural supports conceptual.
span.quote: the relationship between conceptual and procedural knowledge is bi-directional, it is not always symmetrical, and that, at times, conceptual knowledge is stronger and more consistent in supporting procedural knowledge, than the reverse.

span.label: The paper's answer to its own title is that teachers need conceptual AND procedural knowledge, with the timing and placement left to the teacher's professional judgement.
span.quote: In answer to the title of this article it should be Conceptual knowledge and Procedural knowledge, the when and where, that is determined by the professional call of the teacher.

span.label: Because both knowledge types can occupy different points on a quality continuum, the dichotomy between conceptual and procedural knowledge is judged fundamentally unsound.
span.quote: Kieran (2013) declared the dichotomy between them to be fundamentally unsound.

span.label: concept
span.quote: a concept can be defined as “a mental representation that embodies all the essential features of an object, a situation, or an idea.

span.label: conceptual knowledge
span.quote: Conceptual knowledge (notably characterised by Skemp, 1978, as Relational Knowledge) may be visualised as a connecting web of relationships

span.label: procedure
span.quote: Procedures are a series of steps and/or actions employed to achieve a task or reach a

span.label: procedural knowledge
span.quote: as the capacity to follow steps in sequence to solve mathematical problems or reach a mathematical goal.

span.label: routine expertise
span.quote: Routine expertise is where there is a superficial conceptual and/or procedural knowledge, which is able to be applied to familiar situations, but not unfamiliar ones, or to new tasks.

span.label: adaptive expertise
span.quote: Adaptive expertise is where both conceptual and procedural knowledge is deep, and where that knowledge can be aplied creatively, flexibly and appropriately to all situations, familiar or new.

span.label: cognitive interference
span.quote: Cognitive interference, considered by Pesek and Kirshner as being the more important interference, is when previous understandings of something are so poweful they obtrude into subsequent learning.

span.label: attitudinal interference
span.quote: Attitudinal interference is where a student’s previously acquired opinions and attitudes block comprehensive engagement with a topic and therefore impede potential for learning (Pesek & Kirshner, 2000).

span.label: iterative view of the conceptual-procedural relationship
span.term: iterative view of the conceptual-procedural relationship
span.quote: the iterative view where the causal relationship is seen as being bi-directional, that is, increases in one, generates increases in the other.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.14221/ajte.2021v46n2.4.
